finding.headline: At 79 and still working, the 401(k) catch-up rules for age 50 and up apply to this household.
details: For 2027, people aged 50 and over can contribute up to $34,000 a year to a 401(k), starting in 2027, under the general catch-up rule.
The IRA limit remains $7,500, and the IRA catch-up for people aged 50 and over remains $1,100.
Medicare starts at age 65. If you miss your 7-month Initial Enrollment Period, you may have to wait to sign up and pay a monthly late enrollment penalty that grows the longer you wait.

finding.headline: This household has no children, pets, or college costs, so family costs are $0.
details: Once retired, the basic yearly costs are about $40,000, or $3,333 a month.
Housing is the largest basic cost at $23,580 a year. Health costs are $6,240 a year, and health premiums before Medicare at age 65 are $10,000 a year.

finding.headline: Plan for your money to last to age 95.
details: At age 95, there is about a 22% chance you are still alive, so the plan should cover at least 15 years of retirement after you stop work at 80.
Your life expectancy is about 10.9 years from now, so plan for more than that, since money that runs short late in life is the bigger risk.

finding.headline: About 16% of your pay goes to tax now, and about 10% of withdrawals in retirement.
details: Now, you pay about $7,705 in tax on $48,000 of pay. In retirement, the plan estimates $3,282 a year in tax.

Almost all your savings sit in a 401(k) or similar pre-tax account, so withdrawals are taxed as income. The plan draws on taxable savings and cash first, then the pre-tax account, and Roth accounts last.
This is a rough guide, not tax advice. Check the order of withdrawals with a tax professional before you act.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.
Your spending now is about $18,505 a year more than your take-home pay, so until you retire the plan takes that from your savings each year. If that is wrong, change your spending now or your pay.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.
You already get Social Security (from 70): the plan uses the $24,000 a year you gave.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 95. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
